q: The SI unit of magnetic flux density (B) is the:
x: Magnetic flux density is measured in tesla (T). The weber is the unit of magnetic flux, the henry of inductance, and the gauss is a smaller non-SI unit.

q: A charged particle enters a uniform magnetic field moving at right angles to the field. Its path in the field is:
x: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to the velocity and constant in size, so it acts as a centripetal force and the particle moves in a circle. A helix happens only when the velocity has a component along the field.

q: One tesla is equal to:
x: From F = BIL, B = F/(IL), so 1 T = 1 N / (1 A × 1 m) = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹. The N C⁻¹ is the unit of electric field strength.

q: A particle of mass m and charge q moves with speed v at right angles to a uniform field B. The radius of its circular path is:
x: The magnetic force provides the centripetal force: qvB = mv²/r, so r = mv/(qB).

q: Magnetic flux density can also be expressed in which unit?
x: B is flux per unit area perpendicular to the field, B = Φ/A, so 1 T = 1 Wb m⁻². A weber per second is a volt.

q: A charged particle moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. If its speed is doubled, the radius of the circle:
x: r = mv/(qB) is directly proportional to v, so doubling the speed doubles the radius.

q: The magnetic flux density is 1 tesla when a straight conductor 1 m long, carrying 1 A at right angles to the field, experiences a force of:
x: Using F = BIL with B = 1 T, I = 1 A and L = 1 m gives F = 1 N. This is the definition of the tesla.

q: A beam of electrons moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. If the magnetic flux density is doubled at the same speed, the radius becomes:
x: r = mv/(qB) is inversely proportional to B, so doubling B halves the radius.

q: The gauss (G) is a smaller unit of magnetic flux density. The correct relation is:
x: 1 gauss = 10⁻⁴ T, so one tesla is 10⁴ gauss. Writing 1 T = 10⁻⁴ G turns the relation upside down.

q: A particle of mass 1.6 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and charge 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C moves at 10⁶ m s⁻¹ at right angles to a uniform field of 0.1 T. The radius of its path is:
A straight wire 0.2 m long carries a current of 4 A at right angles to a uniform magnetic field of 0.5 T. The force on the wire is:

A proton and a deuteron (same charge, twice the proton's mass) enter the same uniform magnetic field at right angles, with the same speed. The ratio of the radius for the deuteron to that for the proton is:
x: r = mv/(qB). With the same v, q and B, r is proportional to m, so the deuteron's radius is twice the proton's.

q: A wire 0.1 m long carrying 5 A lies at 30° to a uniform magnetic field of 2 T. The force on it is: (sin 30° = 0.5, cos 30° = 0.87)
x: F = BIL sin θ = 2 × 5 × 0.1 × 0.5 = 0.5 N. Using cos 30° gives 0.87 N, and ignoring the angle gives 1 N.

q: A proton and an alpha particle (four times the mass, twice the charge) enter the same uniform field at right angles with the same kinetic energy. The ratio of the alpha particle's radius to the proton's radius is:
x: Momentum mv = √(2mK), so r = √(2mK)/(qB). For the alpha particle √(4m) = 2√m and q = 2e, so the factors of 2 cancel and the radii are equal.

q: Expressed in SI base units, the tesla is:
x: 1 T = 1 N A⁻¹ m⁻¹ and 1 N = 1 kg m s⁻², so 1 T = kg m s⁻² / (A m) = kg s⁻² A⁻¹. Forgetting to cancel the metre gives kg m s⁻² A⁻¹.

q: A charged particle moves in a circle at right angles to a uniform magnetic field. The time it takes to complete one revolution:
o: Is directly proportional to its speed
Is inversely proportional to its speed
Does not depend on its speed
Is proportional to the square of its speed
x: T = 2πr/v and r = mv/(qB), so T = 2πm/(qB). A faster particle moves in a proportionally larger circle, so the time per revolution is unchanged.

q: Magnetic flux density and magnetic flux are, respectively:
x: B has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector. Flux Φ = B·A is the dot product of two vectors, which is a scalar.

q: An electron beam with speed v moves in a circle of radius r at right angles to a uniform field B. The charge-to-mass ratio e/m of the electron is:
x: From evB = mv²/r, e/m = v/(Br). This is the principle of the e/m experiment.

q: A straight current-carrying wire is placed parallel to a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic force on the wire is:
x: F = BIL sin θ, and θ = 0° when the wire is parallel to the field, so sin θ = 0 and the force is zero. The force is maximum (BIL) when the wire is perpendicular to the field.

q: An electron and a proton enter the same uniform magnetic field with the same velocity at right angles to the field. Which statement is correct?
o: They curve in opposite senses, and the electron's circle is much smaller
They curve in the same sense, with equal radii
They curve in opposite senses, with equal radii
They curve in the same sense, and the electron's circle is much larger
x: Opposite charges feel opposite forces, so they turn opposite ways. With equal v, q and B, r = mv/(qB) is proportional to mass, and the electron is far lighter, so its circle is much smaller.

q: The SI unit of magnetic flux is the:
x: Magnetic flux Φ is measured in webers (Wb). The tesla is the unit of magnetic flux density, which is flux per unit area.

q: The magnitude of the magnetic force on a charge q moving with speed v at an angle θ to a uniform field B is:
x: F = qvB sin θ, the magnitude of q(v × B). It is greatest when the charge moves at right angles to the field.

q: A flat coil is placed in a uniform magnetic field. The magnetic flux through it is greatest when:
o: The plane of the coil is parallel to the field
The plane of the coil is at 45° to the field
The plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field
The coil is moved along the field lines
x: Φ = BA cos θ, where θ is the angle between B and the normal to the coil. When the plane is perpendicular to B, the normal is along B, θ = 0° and Φ = BA, the maximum.

q: A proton is fired exactly along the direction of a uniform magnetic field. Its motion in the field is:
o: A circle at right angles to the field
A circle in the plane containing the field
A straight line at constant speed
A straight line with increasing speed
x: With θ = 0°, F = qvB sin 0° = 0, so no force acts and the proton keeps moving in a straight line at constant speed.

q: A coil of area A in a uniform field B is turned from a position where its plane is perpendicular to B to a position where its plane is parallel to B. The flux through it changes from:
x: With the plane perpendicular to B the field passes straight through, Φ = BA. With the plane parallel to B no field lines cross it, so Φ = 0.

q: According to Ampère's law, the sum of B·ΔL taken around any closed path is equal to:
o: μ₀ times the current divided by the length of the path
ε₀ times the total current enclosed by the path
μ₀ times the total current enclosed by the path
x: Ampère's law: ΣB·ΔL = μ₀ × (net current enclosed). It is zero only when the path encloses no net current, and ε₀ belongs to electrostatics, not magnetism.

q: A long solenoid 0.5 m long has 1000 turns and carries 2 A. The magnetic field inside it is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
x: n = N/ℓ = 1000/0.5 = 2000 turns m⁻¹, so B = μ₀nI = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2000 × 2 = 1.6π × 10⁻³ T. Using N = 1000 as the turns per metre gives 0.8π × 10⁻³ T.

q: A long solenoid is rewound on the same tube so that it has twice as many turns over the same length, and the current is halved. The field inside it:
x: B = μ₀nI. Doubling n and halving I leaves the product nI, and so B, unchanged. Changing only one of them would double or halve the field.

q: A long straight wire carries 5 A. A closed loop is drawn near the wire so that the wire passes outside the loop. Around this loop, ΣB·ΔL is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
x: Ampère's law counts only the current enclosed by the path. The wire is outside the loop, so the enclosed current is zero and ΣB·ΔL = 0, even though B itself is not zero along the loop. Using 5 A gives μ₀ × 5 = 2π × 10⁻⁶ T m.

q: A closed path encloses two long parallel wires, one carrying 3 A upward and the other 5 A downward. ΣB·ΔL around the path has magnitude (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
x: The currents are opposite, so the net enclosed current is 5 − 3 = 2 A and ΣB·ΔL = μ₀ × 2 = 8π × 10⁻⁷ T m. Adding the currents (8 A) gives 32π × 10⁻⁷ T m.

q: A long straight wire carries a current of 10 A. The magnetic field at a distance of 2 cm from the wire is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
x: B = μ₀I/(2πr) = (4π × 10⁻⁷ × 10)/(2π × 0.02) = 2 × 10⁻⁶/0.02 = 1 × 10⁻⁴ T. Leaving r as 2 instead of 0.02 m gives 1 × 10⁻⁶ T; dropping the 2 in 2πr gives 2 × 10⁻⁴ T.

q: A solenoid 40 cm long must produce a field of 2π × 10⁻³ T inside it with a current of 5 A. The number of turns needed is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
x: n = B/(μ₀I) = 2π × 10⁻³/(4π × 10⁻⁷ × 5) = 1000 turns per metre, so N = nℓ = 1000 × 0.4 = 400 turns. Stopping at n gives 1000; dividing n by ℓ instead of multiplying gives 2500.

q: The magnetic field well inside a long current-carrying solenoid is:
o: strongest near the wall and zero on the axis
uniform and directed along the axis
directed in circles around the axis
x: Inside a long solenoid the field lines are straight, parallel to the axis and evenly spaced, so the field is uniform, B = μ₀nI. Circles around a conductor describe the field of a single straight wire.

q: To find the field of a long solenoid, Ampère's law is applied to a rectangular path with one long side inside the solenoid along the axis and the opposite side outside. Which part of the path gives a non-zero B·ΔL?
o: only the side outside the solenoid
only the side inside the solenoid, parallel to the axis
only the two sides perpendicular to the axis
x: Outside a long solenoid B ≈ 0, and along the two perpendicular sides B is at right angles to ΔL (or zero outside), so B·ΔL = 0 there. Only the inside side contributes, giving Bℓ = μ₀NI and B = μ₀nI.

q: Two long solenoids have the same number of turns per metre and carry the same current, but the radius of the first is twice that of the second. The ratio of the fields inside them, B₁ : B₂, is:
x: For a long solenoid B = μ₀nI, which does not depend on the radius or cross-sectional area. With the same n and I the fields are equal. Thinking B grows with area gives 4 : 1.

q: A long solenoid is made by winding a single layer of insulated wire of diameter 0.5 mm, turns touching each other, and it carries 1 A. The field inside is (μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹):
x: Each turn takes 0.5 mm of length, so n = 1/(0.5 × 10⁻³) = 2000 turns m⁻¹ and B = μ₀nI = 4π × 10⁻⁷ × 2000 × 1 = 8π × 10⁻⁴ T. Using the radius 0.25 mm doubles n and gives 1.6π × 10⁻³ T.

q: At a distance r from a long straight wire carrying current I the field is B₀. At a distance 3r from the wire, when the current is 3I, the field is:
x: B = μ₀I/(2πr) is proportional to I/r. Tripling both I and r leaves I/r, and so the field, unchanged at B₀. Multiplying the two changes instead of dividing gives 9B₀.

q: A beam of charged particles passes undeflected through a velocity selector with crossed fields E = 2 × 10⁴ V m⁻¹ and B = 0.1 T, both at right angles to the beam. The speed of the particles is:
x: No deflection means qE = qvB, so v = E/B = 2 × 10⁴/0.1 = 2 × 10⁵ m s⁻¹. Multiplying E by B gives 2 × 10³ m s⁻¹, and B/E gives 5 × 10⁻⁶ m s⁻¹.

q: To convert a moving-coil galvanometer into an ammeter, we connect:
o: a low resistance in parallel with it
a high resistance in series with it
a low resistance in series with it
a high resistance in parallel with it
x: A low-resistance shunt in parallel carries most of the current, so only the full-scale current passes through the coil. A high resistance in series is used to make a voltmeter.

q: In a moving-coil galvanometer the pole pieces are concave and a soft-iron cylinder sits inside the coil, so the field is radial. This is done so that:
o: the coil does not rotate at all
the plane of the coil always lies along the field, making the deflection proportional to the current
the field at the coil becomes zero
the resistance of the coil is reduced
x: In a radial field the plane of the coil stays parallel to B at every deflection, so the torque BINA does not depend on the angle and the deflection θ is proportional to I, giving an evenly spaced scale.

q: A rectangular coil of 100 turns and area 20 cm² carries 0.5 A in a uniform field of 0.2 T, with the plane of the coil parallel to the field. The torque on the coil is:
x: With the plane parallel to B the torque is maximum: τ = BINA = 0.2 × 0.5 × 100 × 20 × 10⁻⁴ = 2 × 10⁻² N m. Forgetting the 100 turns gives 2 × 10⁻⁴ N m; thinking 'parallel' means no torque gives zero.

q: A coil of 50 turns and area 0.01 m² carries 2 A in a uniform field of 0.5 T. The plane of the coil makes an angle of 60° with the field. The torque on it is (cos 60° = 0.5, sin 60° ≈ 0.87):
x: τ = BINA cos α, where α is the angle between the plane of the coil and the field: τ = 0.5 × 2 × 50 × 0.01 × 0.5 = 0.25 N m. Using sin 60° instead gives about 0.43 N m; the maximum torque would be 0.5 N m.

q: A galvanometer of resistance 99 Ω gives full-scale deflection with 10 mA. The shunt needed to convert it into an ammeter of range 0-1 A is:
x: Rs = IgRg/(I − Ig) = (0.01 × 99)/(1 − 0.01) = 0.99/0.99 = 1 Ω. Dividing by I instead of (I − Ig) gives 0.99 Ω.

q: A galvanometer of resistance 50 Ω gives full-scale deflection with 1 mA. The resistance to be connected in series to make a voltmeter of range 0-10 V is:
x: R = V/Ig − Rg = 10/(1 × 10⁻³) − 50 = 10000 − 50 = 9950 Ω. Forgetting to subtract the galvanometer's own resistance gives 10000 Ω.

q: A galvanometer has a resistance of 90 Ω. The shunt that makes the full-scale current of the resulting ammeter 10 times the galvanometer's full-scale current is:
x: Only 1/10 of the current goes through the coil, so the shunt carries 9/10: IgRg = 9Ig × Rs, Rs = Rg/(n − 1) = 90/9 = 10 Ω. Dividing by n gives 9 Ω; Rg(n − 1) = 810 Ω is the series resistor rule for a voltmeter.

q: A galvanometer of resistance 99 Ω is fitted with a shunt of 1 Ω to make an ammeter. The resistance of the ammeter is:
x: The coil and shunt are in parallel: R = (99 × 1)/(99 + 1) = 99/100 = 0.99 Ω, a little less than the shunt. Adding them as if in series gives 100 Ω.

q: A voltmeter of total resistance 2000 Ω reads full scale at 2 V. To make it read full scale at 10 V, the extra resistance connected in series with it must be:
x: Full-scale current = 2/2000 = 1 mA. For 10 V the total resistance must be 10/(1 × 10⁻³) = 10000 Ω, so the extra series resistance is 10000 − 2000 = 8000 Ω. Giving the total 10000 Ω as the answer is the usual slip.

q: Which change makes a moving-coil galvanometer more sensitive, so that it gives a larger deflection for the same current?
o: using a stiffer suspension with a larger torsion constant
reducing the area of the coil
increasing the number of turns of the coil
x: At balance BINA = cθ, so θ/I = BNA/c. More turns increase the deflection per unit current; a larger c, smaller A or smaller B all reduce it.

q: The torque on a current-carrying coil in a uniform magnetic field is greatest when:
o: the plane of the coil is perpendicular to the field
the plane of the coil is at 45° to the field
the plane of the coil is parallel to the field
the current in the coil is zero
x: τ = BINA cos α, with α the angle between the plane of the coil and B, is largest when α = 0, i.e. the plane is parallel to the field. When the plane is perpendicular to B the flux is maximum but the torque is zero.

q: A good voltmeter must have a very high resistance because:
o: it then draws very little current, so the potential difference it measures is hardly changed
it then carries a large current safely
it then increases the current in the circuit
it then makes the coil turn faster
x: A voltmeter is connected in parallel. A high resistance draws almost no current from the circuit, so it does not lower the potential difference being measured. An ammeter, in series, needs a very low resistance instead.
